title: Handling Secrets & Sensitive Data 🤫
description: Never hardcode credentials – use environment variables, secure files, and clearing techniques.

slides.title: Hardcoding = Public 🔓
slides.content:
## Your Script Could End Up on GitHub

Never embed passwords, API keys, or tokens directly in the script. Anyone with read access (or version control history) can see them.

Instead, use:
- Environment variables
- Separate config files with restricted permissions
- Secret managers (vault, pass, 1Password CLI)
- Read from stdin or `read -s`

slides.title: Environment Variable Approach
slides.content: Export the secret in your shell, then reference it:
slides.codeSnippet:
export DB_PASS="supersecret"
# In script:
echo "Connecting with $DB_PASS"  # still prints it, better to not echo!

quizData.question: Why is it better to pass secrets via environment variable than a command‑line argument?

options.text: Command‑line arguments may be visible in `ps` output

quizData.explanation: Arguments appear in `ps aux`, potentially exposing secrets to other users. Environment vars are not normally visible to other users (unless `/proc` is exposed).

slides.title: Reading Secrets Securely 🤐
slides.content:
## `read -s` and Prompt

For passwords typed by a user, use `read -sp`. The secret won't echo to the terminal.

Never log or debug‑print the raw password. Clear the variable as soon as possible with `unset` or `passwd=`.

slides.title: Read Password Safely
slides.codeSnippet:
read -sp "Database password: " DB_PASS
echo
# use DB_PASS
# ...
unset DB_PASS

quizData.question: You should always `echo $PASSWORD` for debugging to ensure it's set.
quizData.explanation: Echoing a secret displays it on screen and possibly in logs, defeating security.

slides.title: Config Files: Lock Them Down 📁
slides.content:
## Secure Permissions on Secrets

If you store credentials in a file:
- Set file permissions to `600` or `400`.
- Ensure the directory is not world‑readable.
- Use `source` to load variables, but ensure the file only contains assignments.
- Consider encrypting the file with `gpg` or `openssl`.

slides.title: Load a Restricted Config
slides.codeSnippet:
config="$HOME/.myapprc"
if [ -f "$config" ]; then
  perms=$(stat -c %a "$config")
  if [ "$perms" = "600" ]; then
    source "$config"
  else
    echo "Config has insecure permissions!" >&2
    exit 1
  fi
fi

slides.title: ⚠️ Cleaning Variables
slides.content: `unset` only removes the variable from the current shell; it may remain in memory. For highly sensitive data, consider using `shred` on files, but variables in memory are harder to erase completely.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content: Use `pass` (the standard Unix password manager) or `gpg --decrypt` to fetch secrets on demand rather than storing them in plaintext.
